title: DynamoDB under the hood: partitions, routers and capacity
goal: By the end, you can follow one DynamoDB write from a router to the three copies of its partition, explain why every partition has a ceiling and when it splits, say why one busy record is refused however much capacity the table has, choose between the two ways of paying for capacity, and create a payments table knowing what each setting does.
opening:
Picture a concert hall's box office. Ten windows hand out booked tickets, each for a range of surnames: A to C, D to F. Each serves a hundred people a minute, so the office serves a thousand.

Tonight a tour company booked 300 seats under one name, and its guests come one by one. All of them queue at one window, while nine sit quiet.

The payments app meets the same queue in DynamoDB, a database that Amazon runs for you. Its table may take 40,000 writes a second and uses 6,000, yet updates to one shop's running total are refused. That number looks like one big pool, because it's the only one the screen shows. But DynamoDB cuts each table into pieces, like the windows, and hides them.

In Running MongoDB, we ran every part of a cluster ourselves. DynamoDB has the same parts, out of reach. In this lesson, we'll follow one write through them, find each ceiling, and set up a payments table setting by setting. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A DynamoDB table is set to accept 40,000 write units a second (one unit pays for one small write) and uses about 6,000. Every payment also adds to one record, the running total for the busiest shop, `MERCH#M-0042#TOTAL`. On the busiest shopping day of the year, that one record gets 1,500 updates a second. What happens to them?
options: Nothing bad: 7,500 used of 40,000 is well within the table's limit
DynamoDB gives the record a machine of its own and lends it the table's 32,500 spare units
About 500 a second are refused: one record lives in one piece of the table, and each piece takes at most 1,000 write units a second
DynamoDB cuts the record's piece of the table in two, again and again, until the load fits
warmup.why: The table's capacity is a sum over its pieces, called partitions, and each partition has a ceiling of its own: 1,000 write units a second, however much the table has. One record lives in exactly one partition. DynamoDB can give a busy record a partition to itself (adaptive capacity, in the third section), but that partition still tops out at 1,000, so the second option fails. And cutting a partition divides a range of keys, while one key can't be divided: the 2022 paper on DynamoDB's design says a partition with heavy traffic to a single item won't benefit from a split. So about 500 updates a second are refused, with the reason `TableWriteKeyRangeThroughputExceeded`.

sections.h: One write's journey: a router, a partition and its three copies
sections.body:
Let's follow one payment into DynamoDB. In Key-value stores and DynamoDB basics, the app stored each record as an item, a set of named values called attributes, under a key in two parts. The partition key, such as `ACCT#A-1001`, says whose item it is. The sort key, such as the payment's time, orders the items that share a partition key. The app sent each item with a request called `PutItem`, and never saw a machine.

You can't log into those machines, because AWS (Amazon Web Services, Amazon's business of renting out computers and programs) runs them. So setting up DynamoDB means designing the table and choosing its capacity. Both choices make sense only once you know what runs underneath, which a 2022 research paper by Elhemali and others describes. Let's build it up.

Version 1 is one server holding the whole table. Its limits are the ones Splitting data started from: one disk, one processor, and an outage when it dies.

Version 2 cuts the table into **partitions**. DynamoDB hashes each partition key, turning it into a large number that looks random, and each partition owns one unbroken stretch of those numbers. Splitting data: key ranges, hashes and tenants met these stretches. A partition is stored as a B-tree, a sorted tree that finds a key in a few steps. It lives on the fast flash disk (SSD) of a storage node, one of the machines that hold data. One storage node holds copies of many partitions, from many tables of many customers.

Now every request must find its partition, so a fleet of request routers sits in front. A router checks who sent the request against IAM, AWS's system of accounts and permissions, and caches the answers, so a slow IAM doesn't stall it. It checks the table's budget of capacity, hashes the key and looks the partition up in a partition map. The maps live in MemDS, a service that keeps them in memory, and each router keeps a small cache of them that refreshes in the background.

Version 3 keeps three copies, called replicas, of every partition, one in each of three availability zones. Those are separate data centres in one AWS Region, a city-sized area, so one building losing power leaves two copies. The three run Multi-Paxos, a consensus protocol in the same family as Raft, which the Consensus track builds. By majority vote, they agree on one leader and one order of writes. The leader holds a lease, a right to lead for a few seconds that it keeps renewing. Only the leader takes writes. It appends each write to its write-ahead log, a file where every change is written first, and sends the record to its two peers. It answers once two of the three, itself included, have it on disk.

Reads come in two kinds. A strongly consistent read goes to the leader, which has every write it confirmed. An eventually consistent read, the default, may go to any replica, which is why it can miss a write that just finished. If the leader dies, a follower calls an election, and the winner waits for the old leader's lease to run out, a couple of seconds, before it takes writes.

Version 4 heals quickly. Rebuilding a lost replica means copying its B-tree, which takes minutes. So the leader first adds a log replica, which stores only recent log records. It joins in seconds, and writes can again get two answers of three while the full replica is rebuilt.

In the box office, the router is the usher who points you to a window, and each window is a partition. Its replicas are like three clerks keeping copies of the window's records, one in charge, except that a partition's replicas sit in three buildings.

**A table is a set of key ranges, each with its own three copies and its own ceiling.** The stepper follows one write through that picture. Next, we'll find out where the ceiling sits.

The leader plus one follower is two of three, a majority, so the leader answers OK, and the router returns HTTP 200, the web's code for success. AZ c's copy is a few milliseconds behind. frames.say: AZ b's storage node fails. A follower that stops hearing from the leader first asks the other replica whether it still sees the leader, which avoids needless elections on a flaky link. Then it starts an election and wins it with AZ c's vote. The new leader waits for the old leader's lease to run out, a couple of seconds, before it takes writes or strong reads. Eventually consistent reads never stop. DynamoDB then builds a new replica in place of the dead one.

sections.h: Every partition has a ceiling, so partitions split
sections.body:
Three limits drive everything in this section. A partition serves at most 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units a second, and holds about 10 GB. Key-value stores and DynamoDB basics defined the units. A write unit pays for one write a second of up to 1 KB. A read unit pays for one strongly consistent read a second of up to 4 KB, or two eventually consistent ones. Rebalancing and request routing compared two designs for shards, as partitions are also called: a fixed number of them, or ones that split as they grow. DynamoDB is the second kind, and it splits for three reasons.

The first is the capacity you ask for. A provisioned table, one where you set its read and write units yourself, gets enough partitions at creation to carry them, and each gets an equal share. The paper's example: 3,200 write units need 4 partitions of 800. Raise the table to 3,600 and each share becomes 900. Raise it to 6,000 and four partitions can't carry that, so each splits in two: 8 partitions of 750. Lower it to 5,000 and you keep 8, at 625 each, because partitions only ever split. They never merge.

The second is size. When a partition nears 10 GB it splits in two, and in the original design its share of the table's units was divided between the halves. A table with 1,000 write units and 15 GB had two partitions of 500. A key range taking 800 writes a second was refused writes while the other half sat idle. The paper calls this throughput dilution, throughput being the work done per second.

The third is traffic. When a partition stays busy, DynamoDB splits it for consumption. It cuts at a point chosen from the keys it has seen used, not the middle of the range, so the busy keys land on both sides. That takes minutes. Two patterns can't be helped, and the paper names both. One is a single item that takes all the traffic. The other is a key range written in order, such as one partition key with a time as its sort key. Every new write lands at the same end, however you cut. In the box office, it's one booking name with a long queue: a new window can't split one name.

When a request needs more than its partition or table may give, DynamoDB throttles it. It refuses the request with HTTP 400, the web's code for a request it won't carry out, and changes nothing. The AWS SDK, Amazon's library for calling AWS from your code, retries a throttled request a few times, waiting longer before each try. So you first see slower answers, then an exception. The exception carries `ThrottlingReasons`, which name the limit. `TableWriteKeyRangeThroughputExceeded` means a hot partition. `TableWriteProvisionedThroughputExceeded` means the table used up its provisioned units. A reason that starts with `Index` points at a global secondary index, or GSI (the fourth section). More provisioned capacity fixes the second reason, and does nothing for the first.

**Read the reason before you raise the capacity.**

DynamoDB Local does none of this. It's a single Java program for development. The docs say it ignores provisioned throughput, and it has no partitions, so it never splits and never throttles. The Try-it proves it. To test how your code handles a throttle, use the lab's model or a real table. Next, we'll see how DynamoDB lends a busy partition the table's spare units, and where that help stops.

try.title: Overload a table of 1 write unit in Local, then read a real throttle
steps: With DynamoDB Local still running, read `LocalNeverThrottlesDemo.kt`. It creates a table with one write unit a second, turns off the SDK's retries, and sends 1,000 writes from eight threads, eight lines of work running at once. Predict how many are throttled.
Then read the second block below, from the AWS docs. That's what a throttle looks like on real DynamoDB; Local can't produce one.

code.title: LocalNeverThrottlesDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.shard.l08.demo

import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.AwsBasicCredentials
import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.StaticCredentialsProvider
import software.amazon.awssdk.awscore.retry.AwsRetryStrategy
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.DynamoDbClient
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.AttributeDefinition
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.AttributeValue
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.BillingMode
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.KeySchemaElement
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.KeyType
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.ProvisionedThroughputExceededException
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.ReturnConsumedCapacity
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.ScalarAttributeType
import java.net.URI
import java.util.concurrent.Executors
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.DoubleAdder

/**
 * A table provisioned with ONE write unit a second, then 1,000 writes from eight threads, as fast as
 * they can send them. Real DynamoDB would admit about one a second plus a few hundred saved-up burst units, and
 * throttle the rest. DynamoDB Local is one process with no partitions and no admission control.
 */
fun main() {
    val ddb = DynamoDbClient.builder()
        .endpointOverride(URI.create("http://localhost:8000"))
        .region(Region.US_EAST_1)
        .credentialsProvider(StaticCredentialsProvider.create(AwsBasicCredentials.create("sfz", "sfz")))
        // no SDK retries: a throttle would reach this code instead of being retried quietly
        .overrideConfiguration { it.retryStrategy(AwsRetryStrategy.doNotRetry()) }
        .build()
    val table = "one-wcu"
    if (table in ddb.listTables().tableNames()) ddb.deleteTable { it.tableName(table) }

    // provisioned mode: 1 read unit and 1 write unit a second for the whole table
    ddb.createTable {
        it.tableName(table)
            .attributeDefinitions(AttributeDefinition.builder().attributeName("pk").attributeType(ScalarAttributeType.S).build())
            .keySchema(KeySchemaElement.builder().attributeName("pk").keyType(KeyType.HASH).build())
            .billingMode(BillingMode.PROVISIONED)
            .provisionedThroughput { p -> p.readCapacityUnits(1).writeCapacityUnits(1) }
    }
    val provisioned = ddb.describeTable { it.tableName(table) }.table().provisionedThroughput()
    println("provisioned: ${provisioned.readCapacityUnits()} RCU, ${provisioned.writeCapacityUnits()} WCU")

    val consumed = DoubleAdder()
    val throttled = AtomicInteger()
    val started = System.nanoTime()
    val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)
    for (i in 0 until 1_000) pool.execute {
        try {
            val r = ddb.putItem {
                it.tableName(table)
                    .item(mapOf(
                        "pk" to AttributeValue.fromS("PAY#pay-%06d".format(i)),
                        "amountMinor" to AttributeValue.fromN((500 + i * 7919 % 9501).toString()),
                    ))
                    .returnConsumedCapacity(ReturnConsumedCapacity.TOTAL)
            }
            consumed.add(r.consumedCapacity().capacityUnits())
        } catch (e: ProvisionedThroughputExceededException) {
            throttled.incrementAndGet() // what real DynamoDB sends when a table or a partition is out of tokens
        }
    }
    pool.shutdown()
    pool.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.MINUTES)
    val seconds = (System.nanoTime() - started) / 1e9
    println("wrote 1,000 items in %.1f s, about %,d a second".format(seconds, (1_000 / seconds).toLong()))
    println("write units consumed: %,.1f".format(consumed.sum()))
    println("throttled: $throttled")

    ddb.deleteTable { it.tableName(table) }
    ddb.close()
}

```text
write units consumed: 1,000.0
throttled: 0
```

The rate depends on your machine; the 0 doesn't. The table took 1,000 write units in three seconds against 1 provisioned, because Local ignores provisioned throughput: one Java program, no partitions, no budgets. Real DynamoDB would admit about one write a second plus whatever burst capacity the table had saved (at most 300 units for a table of 1 write unit, as the next section explains), and throttle the rest.

On real DynamoDB, a throttle reaches the SDK as an exception with reasons. This example is from the AWS docs' page on diagnosing throttling (trimmed), not from Local. It's a GSI that ran out of provisioned write units:

```json
{
    "ThrottlingReasons": [
        {
            "reason": "IndexWriteProvisionedThroughputExceeded",
            "resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:us-west-2:123456789012:table/CustomerOrders/index/OrderDateIndex"
        }
    ],
    "awsErrorDetails": {
        "errorCode": "ProvisionedThroughputExceeded",
        "errorMessage": "The level of configured provisioned throughput for the index was exceeded",
        ...
    }
}
```

The HTTP status is 400.

In Kotlin that's a `ProvisionedThroughputExceededException`. A hot partition gives the reason `TableWriteKeyRangeThroughputExceeded`, and an on-demand limit gives a `ThrottlingException`. The reason, not the exception's class, tells you which fix applies.

sections.h: Paying for capacity: set it yourself, or pay per request
sections.body:
Capacity is the number of read and write units DynamoDB lets a table use each second. You choose one of two modes, and the history of the first explains how both behave today.

In provisioned mode you set the units and pay for them by the hour, used or not. DynamoDB's first design, from 2012, enforced each partition's share at the partition with a token bucket: a counter that refills at the share's rate, which each request pays from. When the bucket is empty, requests are refused. The AWS docs' example shows the flaw. A table of 400 write units over 4 partitions gives each 100. Send partition 4 150 writes a second and the others 50 each. Partition 4 refuses 50 a second, while the table is asked for only 300 of its 400.

Burst capacity came first. A partition saves up to 300 seconds of its unused share and spends it on a spike. A partition that ran at 50 of its 100 for five minutes saved 15,000 units, enough for 150 a second for another 300 seconds. Then it throttles again. Burst covers a spike, not a partition that's always busy.

Adaptive capacity came next. Partitioning: consistent hashing and hot keys spread a hot key by hand, and this is DynamoDB doing part of that job for you. When a partition is throttled while the table has unused units, DynamoDB raises that partition's share. The table must stay within its total, and the partition within 1,000 write units. Partition 4 gets its 150, because 50 + 50 + 50 + 150 = 300 fits in 400. The paper says this removed over 99.99% of the throttling caused by uneven traffic. It can also move a very busy item into a partition of its own, so that the item gets the full 1,000. In the box office, it's sending staff from the quiet windows to the busy one, up to what one window can serve.

Today's design is global admission control. A central service tracks each table's budget as tokens. Each request router keeps a local token bucket and refills it from that service every few seconds. Partitions keep buckets of their own as a second line of defence, capped so that no table can take over a storage node. So a hot partition can use the table's spare units at once, and one key above 1,000 write units is still refused. The partition ceiling never moves.

In on-demand mode you set nothing and pay per request. A new on-demand table takes up to 4,000 writes and 12,000 reads a second. After that, DynamoDB admits up to double your previous peak at once, and splits partitions ahead of the next peak. Beyond double, it adds capacity as traffic grows, but the docs warn that you can be throttled if you pass double your previous peak within 30 minutes. A per-table quota caps it, 40,000 units of each by default, and you can set a lower maximum of your own as a guard against a runaway bill. For a launch you know about, you can pre-warm the table by raising its warm throughput, the load it can take at once.

Choose on-demand for new tables, spiky traffic and anything you can't forecast, such as a payments app whose evening peak is ten times its night. Choose provisioned for steady load you can forecast and that runs most of the day, because per unit it costs less. Auto scaling, AWS raising and lowering the units as traffic changes, keeps it close to the load. You can switch a table from provisioned to on-demand up to four times in 24 hours, and back at any time. Next, we'll follow the copies a write makes after its partition has said yes.

sections.h: Work that happens after the write: indexes, streams, expiry, backups and other Regions
sections.body:
Several features copy each write somewhere else after the partition has confirmed it. They do their work afterwards, on their own time, and that explains how each one behaves.

A global secondary index (GSI) is a second copy of the table's items, arranged by another attribute, so you can find items without their partition key. It's the global index from Secondary indexes across shards: a table of its own, partitioned by the indexed attribute, with partitions and ceilings of its own. After a write is confirmed, DynamoDB sends the change on to the index's partitions. DynamoDB single-table design and transactions showed the result: an index can lag behind, so it answers only eventually consistent reads.

That lesson didn't show back-pressure. If an index can't keep up, because it has too few write units or a hot key, DynamoDB throttles writes to the table itself. The exception names the index: `IndexWriteKeyRangeThroughputExceeded`. A hot index key is easy to make by accident: `merchantId` with M-0042, or `status` with only three values. Give each GSI at least the table's write units, and choose its key as carefully as the table's. And every index that holds an item costs a write when the item changes, which the Try-it counts.

DynamoDB Streams is the table's change log. Each insert, update or delete becomes a record, kept for 24 hours and appearing exactly once, in order for each item (not across items). The stream is cut into shards too, each tied to one partition, so it grows shards as the table splits. Another program can read the stream to copy every change somewhere else, such as a reporting copy. As DynamoDB single-table design and transactions warned, a transaction's writes arrive as separate records.

TTL (time to live) deletes items whose expiry attribute has passed. That attribute holds a time as a number of seconds since the start of 1970, which is how computers often count time. The deletes come typically within a few days, and cost no write units. Until then the expired item is still there, so reads must filter it out. The deletes reach the stream marked as service deletions, so a reader can tell them from yours.

Point-in-time recovery keeps continuous backups for 1 to 35 days (35 by default), to the second. A restore builds a new table from partition snapshots plus the write-ahead logs that DynamoDB keeps in S3, Amazon's file storage service. It never touches the live table, which makes it the answer to a bad change that deleted payments.

Global tables copy a table to other Regions, and Many leaders, in the Replication track, took them apart. MREC (multi-Region eventual consistency) accepts writes in every Region and settles conflicts (two Regions changing one item at once) by letting the last writer win. MRSC (multi-Region strong consistency, generally available since June 2025) copies each write to at least one other Region before it answers, across exactly three Regions. Underneath, each Region's copy is an ordinary table, with its own partitions, routers and ceilings. A hot key is as hot in every Region.

Next, we'll put all of this into one command that creates the payments table.

sections.h: Creating the payments table for real, setting by setting
sections.body:
Every setting in a real `create-table` now maps to something above. Here is the payments table from DynamoDB single-table design and transactions, as you'd create it with the AWS CLI:

```bash
aws dynamodb create-table --table-name payments \
  --attribute-definitions \
      AttributeName=pk,AttributeType=S AttributeName=sk,AttributeType=S \
      AttributeName=paymentId,AttributeType=S AttributeName=merchantId,AttributeType=S \
      AttributeName=status,AttributeType=S AttributeName=createdAt,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema AttributeName=pk,KeyType=HASH AttributeName=sk,KeyType=RANGE \
  --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST \
  --on-demand-throughput MaxReadRequestUnits=24000,MaxWriteRequestUnits=8000 \
  --warm-throughput ReadUnitsPerSecond=24000,WriteUnitsPerSecond=8000 \
  --global-secondary-indexes file://payments-gsis.json \
  --stream-specification StreamEnabled=true,StreamViewType=NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES \
  --deletion-protection-enabled
aws dynamodb update-time-to-live --table-name payments \
  --time-to-live-specification Enabled=true,AttributeName=expiresAt
aws dynamodb update-continuous-backups --table-name payments \
  --point-in-time-recovery-specification PointInTimeRecoveryEnabled=true,RecoveryPeriodInDays=35
```

The key schema, the part that names the keys, is that lesson's design: `pk` spreads accounts over partitions, and `sk` orders each account's items. Only key attributes are declared; every other attribute is up to each item. `PAY_PER_REQUEST` is on-demand, right for a payments app whose busiest day is many times its quietest night. The on-demand maximum caps the table at 8,000 writes a second, so a runaway retry loop gets throttled instead of billed; leave room above the real peak. Warm throughput lets a new table take the expected launch peak at once instead of growing into it. AWS charges for raising it, and it can't be lowered.

The file holds the two GSIs, `byPayment` and `byMerchant`, with the sort key of several attributes from that lesson, and each costs a write for every item it holds. The stream holds each item's old and new version. Another program can read it to copy every change elsewhere, for example into Kafka, a program that keeps a log of messages for others to read. Deletion protection makes `delete-table` fail until someone turns it off. TTL and point-in-time recovery need calls of their own.

Most teams keep a table's settings in a file and let a tool create it. Terraform, a popular tool that creates cloud resources from text files, describes the same table like this:

```text
resource "aws_dynamodb_table" "payments" {
  name                        = "payments"
  billing_mode                = "PAY_PER_REQUEST"
  hash_key                    = "pk"
  range_key                   = "sk"
  stream_enabled              = true
  stream_view_type            = "NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES"
  deletion_protection_enabled = true

  attribute {
    name = "pk"
    type = "S"
  }
  # ...one attribute block each for sk, paymentId, merchantId, status, createdAt

  on_demand_throughput {
    max_read_request_units  = 24000
    max_write_request_units = 8000
  }
  global_secondary_index {
    name            = "byPayment"
    projection_type = "ALL"
    key_schema {
      attribute_name = "paymentId"
      key_type       = "HASH"
    }
    key_schema {
      attribute_name = "sk"
      key_type       = "RANGE"
    }
  }
  # ...byMerchant: merchantId HASH, then status and createdAt RANGE
  ttl {
    attribute_name = "expiresAt"
    enabled        = true
  }
  point_in_time_recovery {
    enabled                 = true
    recovery_period_in_days = 35
  }
}
```

For steady load, provisioned is the other shape: `--provisioned-throughput` on the table and on each GSI, auto scaling set up through Application Auto Scaling, and every GSI's write units at least the table's. Before real payments arrive, check the key against your peak per key: no item and no partition key above 1,000 write units. Turn on Contributor Insights, a report in CloudWatch (AWS's monitoring service) of the busiest and most throttled keys, and set alarms on the throttle counts, split by reason. The Try-it runs the command against Local, and shows which settings Local really honours.

compare.title: The same jobs in a MongoDB sharded cluster and in DynamoDB

a.label: MongoDB sharded cluster (lesson 7)
a.src:
route a request   mongos, which you run, near the app
the map           config server replica set: config.chunks
unit of data      chunk: a range of shard key values, 128 MB
replication       replica set per shard: primary + oplog,
                  Raft-derived elections, w: "majority"
split             balancer cuts ranges as it migrates them
move              balancer: moveRange, 3 x chunk size apart
hot single key    one chunk on one shard; jumbo if it grows
you choose        shard key, members, oplog size, hardware

b.label: DynamoDB (this lesson)
b.src:
route a request   request routers, run by AWS
the map           partition metadata in MemDS
unit of data      partition: a hash range, about 10 GB,
                  3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU
replication       three replicas in three AZs: Multi-Paxos
                  leader, write acked by 2 of 3
split             by size, by throughput, for consumption
move              DynamoDB places replicas by load
hot single key    one partition: 1,000 WCU, then throttled
you choose        key design, capacity mode, indexes

compare.note: The machinery has the same shape: a router that looks keys up in a map kept in copied metadata, ranges of keys as the unit that gets placed and moved, and a group of copies per range that agrees on the order of writes. The difference is who runs it and what you may touch. In MongoDB you run every box, so you size the oplog, place the members and choose when the balancer works; the shard key is the one decision that's costly to undo. In DynamoDB you touch only the key and the capacity, and in return you get hard ceilings per partition that no setting can raise. A hot key fails the same way in both: one key can't be split, so its writes stay with one machine's leader.

worked.title: Size a payments table from the numbers, then check the hot keys

lab.title: Model DynamoDB partitions: splits, throttling, burst, adaptive capacity and on-demand
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. No Docker needed. All eleven fail with `NotImplementedError`, Kotlin's way of saying a function has no body yet.

Read `PartitionModel.kt`. The limits, `partitionOf` (equal slices of the hash space, so a split turns slice i into 2i and 2i + 1), the table classes and their `updateProvisioned` and `grow` are given. The model counts writes only; reads work the same way with 3,000.

Write `Partitions.forNewTable` and `Partitions.afterSplits`. Three tests pass, including the paper's example: 3,200 write units make 4 partitions of 800, 6,000 make 8 of 750, and lowering to 5,000 keeps 8, at 625.

Write `ProvisionedTable.serve`, in the order its KDoc (the comment above it) gives: share, adaptive capacity, burst, save, throttle. The docs' example now behaves as in the text. Without adaptive capacity, the fourth partition (index 3) refuses 50 a second while the table uses only 250 of its 400. Burst covers a spike of 150 a second for exactly 300 seconds, and with adaptive capacity nothing is throttled.
Write `OnDemandTable.serve`. The on-demand tests pass: a new table admits 4,000 of 6,000, then 8,000 once its peak is 4,000. The hot key test passes in both modes, with 500 throttled every second.

Experiment: in the hot key test, raise the provisioned table to 400,000 write units. It still throttles 5,000 over ten seconds. Then spread the key over four keys (`MERCH#M-0042#TOTAL#0` to `#3`, 375 each) and watch it drop to 0.
hints: Round up with Longs: `(a + b - 1) / b`. `bytes` is a `Long`, and `rcu` and `wcu` fit in one once you call `toLong()`.
Demand per partition: `val demand = IntArray(partitions); for ((pk, units) in writes) demand[partitionOf(pk, partitions)] += units`.
`minOf` takes three arguments: `minOf(demand[p], share, PARTITION_MAX_WCU)`. The adaptive and burst extras are each `minOf(what's still wanted, room under the partition max, what's available)`.
`burst` is a `MutableList<Long>`. Convert with `toLong()` and `toInt()` at the edges, and cap it at `BURST_SECONDS.toLong() * share`.

On-demand, take the excess back from the highest partition down: `for (p in partitions - 1 downTo 0)`. Split ahead with `Partitions.afterSplits(partitions, (ceiling() + PARTITION_MAX_WCU - 1) / PARTITION_MAX_WCU)` after updating `previousPeak`.

Then add one line each: a partition's three ceilings, what a new on-demand table admits and how that grows, and why one hot item is throttled whatever the table's capacity.

aws dynamodb create-table --table-name payments \
  --attribute-definitions AttributeName=pk,AttributeType=S AttributeName=sk,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema AttributeName=pk,KeyType=HASH AttributeName=sk,KeyType=RANGE \

aws dynamodb update-continuous-backups --table-name payments \

# a partition: 3,000 RCU, 1,000 WCU, about 10 GB; past those it splits (or throttles)
# on-demand: 4,000 writes and 12,000 reads a second when new, then double the
#   previous peak at once; beyond double within 30 minutes may throttle
# one hot item: one key lives in one partition, and no split can divide a key,
#   so it gets 1,000 WCU at most

recap: A request goes to any request router, which checks who sent it, takes units from the table's budget, hashes the partition key and finds the partition in a map cached from MemDS.

Each partition is three replicas in three availability zones that agree on a leader with Multi-Paxos. The leader takes writes and strongly consistent reads, and answers once 2 of 3 have the log record; an eventually consistent read may come from any replica.

A partition takes at most 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units a second, and holds about 10 GB. Partitions split by size, by the capacity you set and by traffic, and never merge. No split helps one hot item or a key range written in order.

A throttle refuses the request with HTTP 400, and `ThrottlingReasons` names the limit. Provisioned tables gained burst (300 seconds of savings), adaptive capacity (the table's spare units for a hot partition) and global admission control; on-demand starts at 4,000 writes a second and admits double the previous peak.

Indexes, streams, TTL, backups and global tables work after the partition has said yes. A GSI lags and can throttle the table's writes, a stream keeps each item's changes in order for 24 hours, and global tables run these same partitions in every Region.

The limit: no setting raises a partition's ceiling, so one key's writes top out at 1,000 units a second in every mode. And DynamoDB Local accepts every setting but models no partitions, splits or throttles, so it can't warn you.
closing:
We started with a box office where one booking name kept a queue at one window while nine sat idle. DynamoDB works the same way: a table's capacity is a sum of partition ceilings, and one record lives behind one of them.

If you have an AWS account, open a DynamoDB table's monitoring page and look for throttled requests. Then ask which key they belong to, and whether more capacity could ever help it.

Next, we'll look inside a search cluster, and find out why a search for one word has to ask every machine.

quiz.q: A provisioned table is created at 3,200 write units, raised to 6,000 for a sale, then lowered to 5,000. How many partitions does it have, and what is each partition's share?
options: 4 partitions of 1,250
5 partitions of 1,000
8 partitions of 625
6 partitions of about 833
quiz.why: 3,200 write units need 4 partitions of 800. 6,000 doesn't fit in 4 at 1,000 each, so each splits in two: 8 of 750. Lowering to 5,000 doesn't merge anything, so it stays at 8, each with 625. Five or six partitions can't happen, because splits go in twos, and 1,250 per partition is above the ceiling of 1,000. This is the paper's example, and the lab's first tests check it.

quiz.q: The app updates a payment to SETTLED, gets HTTP 200, and at once reads it back with a default `GetItem`. It sees AUTHORIZED. What happened?
options: The update wasn't safe yet: HTTP 200 only means the router queued it
The default read is eventually consistent, so a replica that hasn't applied the update yet may answer it; `ConsistentRead` would have gone to the leader
A GSI answered the read
The update went to a different partition than the read
quiz.why: HTTP 200 means two of the three replicas have the update in their logs, so it's safe on disk, and the first option fails. But a default read may be answered by any replica, including the third, which can be a few milliseconds behind. With `ConsistentRead`, the read goes to the leader, which has every confirmed write, and costs 1 read unit instead of half. `GetItem` never reads a GSI, and one key always maps to one partition.

quiz.q: Writes to the table are throttled although it uses a third of its provisioned write units. The reason is `IndexWriteKeyRangeThroughputExceeded` on `byStatus`, a GSI keyed on `status` (AUTHORIZED, SETTLED or FAILED). What is the fix?
options: Raise the table's provisioned write units
Switch the table to on-demand
Change the index's key so its writes spread over many values (or add a shard suffix), because one status value is one hot key range on the index
Retry the writes with longer waits between tries
quiz.why: This is GSI back-pressure: the index can't take the updates, so DynamoDB throttles writes to the table, and the reason names the index. `KeyRange` means a partition ceiling, not a capacity setting, so more units or on-demand change nothing, and that rules out the two tempting first options: every SETTLED payment still lands on one index key. With only three values, the busiest key gets a large share of all writes. Spread the key; retries only add load.

quiz.q: An on-demand table has served a peak of 10,000 writes a second. A product launch suddenly sends 50,000 a second. What should you expect?
options: All 50,000 are admitted at once: on-demand has no limits
About 20,000 a second are admitted at once, double the previous peak; the rest may be throttled while DynamoDB adds capacity, so pre-warm the table before the launch
Exactly 10,000 a second, the previous peak, until you raise it
The table switches itself to provisioned mode
quiz.why: On-demand takes up to double the previous peak at once. Above that, DynamoDB adds capacity as traffic grows, but the docs warn of throttling if you pass double the previous peak within 30 minutes. Warm throughput exists for exactly this: raise it before the launch, and the table can take the new peak at once. The per-table quota, 40,000 units by default, would also cap 50,000 until it's raised. The first option is the trap: on-demand removes the setting, not the limits.

quiz.q: In Partitioning: consistent hashing and hot keys, you spread M-0042's 4,000 writes a second over `MERCH#M-0042#0` to `#9`. In this lesson's picture, why does that work when adaptive capacity alone didn't?
options: Ten keys hash to ten places in the hash space, so splits can put them on different partitions, each with its own ceiling of 1,000 write units; adaptive capacity only raises one partition's share, never above 1,000
Adaptive capacity only works for reads
Keys with a suffix are stored in a different table with more capacity
Write sharding turns the writes into eventually consistent ones, which cost half
quiz.why: A partition key's hash decides its partition, so ten suffixes are ten keys spread over the hash space. DynamoDB can split for consumption and put them on different partitions, and the busiest one in that lesson's demo got 454 writes, under the ceiling. Adaptive capacity lends a hot partition the table's unused units, but the ceiling of 1,000 write units never moves, and one key can't be split. Consistency only applies to reads.

flashcards.front: What does a DynamoDB request router do?
flashcards.back: It checks who sent the request (with cached IAM answers), takes units from the table's budget, hashes the partition key, finds the partition in its map (cached from MemDS) and sends the request to that partition's leader or a replica.

flashcards.front: How is a DynamoDB partition copied?
flashcards.back: Three replicas in three availability zones agree on a leader with Multi-Paxos. The leader takes writes and strong reads; a write is confirmed when 2 of 3 have the log record.
3,000 read units and 1,000 write units a second, and about 10 GB. Splits keep each partition under them; a single key can never go past them.

flashcards.front: Which load can't a partition split help?
flashcards.back: One item that takes all the traffic, and a key range written in order (for example a time as the sort key), where every new write lands at the same end.

flashcards.front: What do burst and adaptive capacity do?
flashcards.back: Burst: a partition spends up to 300 seconds of its saved, unused share on a spike. Adaptive: a throttled partition gets the table's unused units, within the table's total and 1,000 write units per partition.

flashcards.front: What does a new on-demand table admit, and how does that grow?
flashcards.back: 4,000 writes and 12,000 reads a second; then up to double the previous peak at once. Passing double within 30 minutes may be throttled, so pre-warm with warm throughput.

flashcards.front: What does DynamoDB Local not model?
flashcards.back: Partitions, splits, provisioned throughput, throttling and point-in-time recovery. It's one program for development.

terms.plain: The front-end program that checks who sent each request, checks the table's budget and sends the request to the partition that owns the key.
One stretch of hashed partition keys, held by three replicas, with its own ceiling: 3,000 read units, 1,000 write units and about 10 GB.
A right to lead for a few seconds that the leader keeps renewing; a new leader waits for the old lease to run out before it takes writes.
DynamoDB refusing a request (HTTP 400) because a partition, the table or a quota has no capacity left this second.
Splitting a busy partition at a key chosen from the traffic it has seen, so the load lands on both halves.
Giving a hot partition the table's unused units, within the table's total and the partition's ceiling.
Token buckets for each table, kept by the request routers and refilled from a central service, which decide what is let in.
Throttling of the table's writes because a global secondary index can't keep up with the updates.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate says: "We're on on-demand now, so we can't be throttled. Throttling is a provisioned-mode problem." Explain what a partition is, which limits still apply in on-demand mode, and what you'd check when throttles appear.
explain_back.answer: DynamoDB cuts every table into partitions. Each one is a stretch of hashed partition keys, held by three replicas in three availability zones, with a leader that takes the writes. Every partition has fixed ceilings in both modes: 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units a second, and about 10 GB. On-demand removes the number we used to set, but not those ceilings, and it adds two limits of its own. It admits up to double the previous peak at once, and may throttle if we pass double within 30 minutes. And there's a quota per table, 40,000 units by default, plus any maximum we set. So a single hot item, such as a shop's running total at 1,500 writes a second, is throttled in on-demand exactly as in provisioned, because one key lives in one partition and no split can divide it. A GSI with an uneven key throttles our writes too. When throttles appear, I'd read the `ThrottlingReasons` first. A `KeyRange` reason means a hot key or range, so we fix the key or shard it. A reason about the on-demand maximum or an account limit means a limit we can raise, and for a launch I'd pre-warm the table. Then I'd turn on Contributor Insights to find the keys.

deeper.body:
The paper spends as much time on correctness as on speed. The core replication protocol is written in TLA+, a language for describing a protocol so that a program can check every possible order of events, and new features that touch it go into that description first. Every log record and message carries a checksum, a short number worked out from its bytes that changes if any byte does. Logs are archived to S3 with a list of what each archive holds, and the archiver checks that every entry belongs to the right table and partition and that no sequence number is missing. A background scrub compares the three live replicas with each other, and with a replica rebuilt offline from the archived logs, to catch bits that silently flip on a disk.

Backups use the same logs. On-demand backups and point-in-time restore are built from the write-ahead logs in S3 plus regular snapshots of each partition, so taking a backup costs the live table nothing. A restore picks, for every partition, the nearest snapshot before the second you asked for, replays the logs up to that second, and writes a new table.

Failure detection has a subtle problem that the paper calls gray failure, and the Faults, time and truth track returns to it. A follower may lose contact with the leader while the leader is fine and serving everyone else. If that follower called an election, it would interrupt a healthy partition, and the new leader would have to wait out the old lease. So a follower that wants an election first asks the other replicas whether they can see the leader, and backs off if they can. That one change cut needless elections sharply.

The metadata story is a lesson in caches. Routers that cache a whole table's map find what they need about 99.75% of the time, but a fleet of cold routers sends every request to the metadata store at once. MemDS answers every lookup, and each router's cache refreshes in the background on every hit, so MemDS sees the same load whether the caches are warm or cold. If a router's map is out of date, the storage node it reached answers with the new membership, or with an error that sends the router back to MemDS. It's the same idea as MongoDB's `StaleConfig` in Running MongoDB.
